content.text: By the end of this lesson, you should be able to:
Explain why aqueous electrolysis is more complex than molten electrolysis
Predict the products at each electrode using the rules
Describe the electrolysis of sodium chloride solution and copper sulfate solution
When an ionic compound is dissolved in water, the water provides additional ions (H⁺ and OH⁻). This makes predicting the products more complicated than for molten compounds.
So in an aqueous solution, there are
At each electrode, there is a choice of which ion is discharged.
At the cathode (choosing between metal ion and H⁺):
More reactive than hydrogen (K, Na, Li, Ca, Mg, Al)
Less reactive than hydrogen (Zn, Fe, Cu, Ag)
More reactive metals hold onto their electrons more tightly, so H⁺ is reduced instead.
At the anode (choosing between non-metal ion and OH⁻):
Halide ions are easier to oxidise than OH⁻ when concentrated.
Hydrogen (if metal is reactive) OR Metal (if less reactive)
Example 1: Electrolysis of Sodium Chloride Solution (Brine)
[DIAGRAM: Electrolysis of brine showing cathode producing H₂, anode producing Cl₂, with NaOH solution remaining]
Na is more reactive than H
Chloride is concentrated, so Cl⁻ is discharged
This is an important industrial process
Example 2: Electrolysis of Dilute Sulfuric Acid
Sulfate ions are very stable and hard to oxidise
Water is decomposed into hydrogen and oxygen
Example 3: Electrolysis of Copper Sulfate Solution
Cu is less reactive than H
Solution becomes acidic (H⁺ and SO₄²⁻ left behind)
Example 4: Electrolysis of Copper Sulfate with Copper Electrodes
Copper moves from anode to cathode
Anode gets smaller, cathode gets bigger
Predict the products of electrolysing potassium bromide solution.
Ions present: K⁺, Br⁻, H⁺, OH⁻
K is more reactive than H, so H⁺ is discharged →
Bromide is a halide and is concentrated, so Br⁻ is discharged →
Write the half-equations for the electrolysis of dilute sodium sulfate solution.
Ions present: Na⁺, SO₄²⁻, H⁺, OH⁻
Na is reactive, so H₂ forms
Sulfate is stable, so O₂ forms
